Greater amberjack Seriola dumerili is a large, fast-growing carangid of considerable commercial and ecological importance throughout subtropical and warm-temperate waters. Laboratory-based studies conducted at 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C] have clarified the species early ontogeny: the time from fertilisation to the actual birthing event is approximately 4.55 days [ab = approximately 4.55 days], with prolarvae emerging from the chorion after a briefer developmental interval of 1.3 days  at the same thermal regime. These values were obtained from controlled rearing trials of fertilised eggs collected from wild broodstock. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae measure 0.287 cm  in total length, representing a modest increase over the total length at the moment of parturition or larval release, which has been reported as 0.356 cm [Lb = 0.356 cm]. This relatively small size at the onset of the lecithotrophic phase underscores the dependence on yolk reserves before the switch to exogenous feeding.

As larvae progress through the pelagic larval phase, growth proceeds rapidly under optimal thermal conditions. Rearing experiments consistently maintain water temperatures at 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C] to standardise developmental comparisons. The time elapsed since the birthing event at which juvenile Seriola dumerili attain puberty has been documented as 3.5 multiplied by 365 days [tp = 3.5 multiplied by 365 days], which translates to roughly three and a half years after parturition. This estimate of the time since birth at puberty aligns with observations from mark-recapture studies indicating that gonadal recrudescence and the onset of vitellogenesis become histologically detectable by the fourth year of life. In terms of body size, the total length recorded at this pubertal transition is approximately 109 cm [Lp = approximately 109 cm], a threshold that reflects the considerable somatic growth required before reproductive maturation is initiated. Puberty in this species therefore represents a major life-history milestone tied closely to both chronological age and hydrodynamic size.

The maximum reported lifespan for Seriola dumerili, derived from otolith-based age validation studies and tag-recapture data under captive conditions, is 17 years [am = 17 years], a longevity that appears consistent across its range when individuals are maintained at a mean water temperature of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C]. Achieving such a long life requires sustained investment in somatic growth and maintenance, with individuals eventually attaining a formidable ultimate total length of 190 cm [Li = 190 cm]. This asymptotic size is among the largest recorded within the genus Seriola. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight associated with such dimensions reaches approximately 80,600 grams [Wwi = approximately 80,600 grams], a body mass that places the greater amberjack among the heaviest pelagic carangids. These upper size limits are seldom observed in heavily exploited populations, where fishing mortality truncates the age structure before individuals can approach their full physiological potential.

Reproductive investment in Seriola dumerili has been quantified through histological examination of ovarian tissue in mature females sampled from the Gulf of Mexico. During the peak spawning season, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a mean value of 5% [GSI = 5%] at a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. Fecundity per individual spawning event has been estimated at approximately 1.2 million eggs per batch [N_R_i = approximately 1.2 million eggs per batch], with females capable of producing 2 such batches each year [F_R_i = 2 such batches each year] during the protracted spawning season that spans the warmer months from April through September. This reproductive strategy yields a substantial annual reproductive output.

From a comparative physiological perspective, the life-history traits of Seriola dumerili reflect a pattern of relatively fast early growth coupled with delayed maturity and exceptional longevity. While the species can reach a body mass exceeding 80,600 grams [Wwi = 80,600 grams] and lengths of 190 cm [Li = 190 cm], its pubertal development at 109 cm [Lp = 109 cm] total length occurs after a substantial post-hatching interval. The total length at hatch of 0.287 cm  and the length at birth of 0.356 cm [Lb = 0.356 cm] illustrate the compact dimensions from which this rapid growth trajectory originates. Under consistent thermal conditions of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C], the species life history unfolds over a 17-year lifespan (17 years) [am = 17 years], with first puberty occurring 1277.5 days since birth [tp = 1277.5 days since birth] and initial hatch events at 1.3 days  after fertilisation. These integrated measurements depict a carangid predator that balances early pelagic vulnerability with eventual predatory dominance in subtropical marine ecosystems.
